title: Winning Planning Interviews
paras: Right — winning planning interviews, graduate to director. A UK guide, for 2026.

Let me take the anxiety out first. In thirty-odd years recruiting planners, I've found the interview rarely decides who gets the job. The employer has usually made their mind up before you sit down — from your application, C-V, LinkedIn, recommendations, the recruiter's feedback, often a reputation that arrived ahead of you. The interview mostly confirms or contradicts that. So don't perform a role; just confirm, calmly, that the person on paper is real.

And they aren't generic — most advice is written by people who've never sat on a planning panel. A council development-management job is a different animal from a housebuilder's land-team interview, and different again from a director role at a consultancy. And it shifts as you rise.

title: Part 1 — How planning recruitment really works
paras: Part one — how recruitment really works. It's rarely one person's call. In a local authority the panel usually has the hiring manager — a team leader or D-M manager — often a senior planner or head of service, sometimes H-R, and for senior posts an elected member. H-R runs the process and guards fairness; they rarely decide, but can veto. The hiring manager's view weighs most, because they have to work with you. The private sector is more commercial and less formal — an associate or director needing a fee-earner, sometimes two stages, technical then cultural, the decision with whoever owns the profit and loss.

Two things follow. Fit matters more than candidates admit — not sameness, but do we want to work with this person, and can we trust them? And technical staff have real influence: a doubtful word from the planner who quizzed you can sink you afterwards, an enthusiastic one carry you. So treat everyone as someone whose opinion counts — the recruiter, and whoever books the room, included.

title: Part 2 — Do your homework
paras: Part two — do your homework. This is where interviews are won, and where average candidates neglect most. Research four things — the employer, the panel, the job and the place — and you'll walk in knowing the role better than half the panel.

The employer, beyond the website: recent schemes and appeal decisions — the Inspectorate names the players, so read their casework — their clients, sectors, trade-press standing, where they're growing. The panel: every interviewer on LinkedIn — background, tenure, R-T-P-I involvement, anything they've written — used lightly, for rapport, never paraded, never personal. The job: take the description apart, essential from desirable, and read the hidden requirements — 'manage a varied caseload' means resilience and organisation, 'work with members and the public' means political awareness and calm. One concrete example ready for each.

And don't underuse the recruiter. A good specialist has placed people here before, and knows the panel, the format, and what sank the last candidate. Ask them straight out what the employer really wants — their fee depends on your success, so a coach on your side, not a gate.

title: Part 3 — The interview changes as you rise
paras: Part three — the interview changes as you rise, and this is the heart of it. The biggest mistake experienced planners make is interviewing the way they did ten years ago, proving technical competence when the panel stopped doubting it long ago. A director candidate proving they understand the N-P-P-F has misread the room. The weight shifts — from technical mastery to leadership, commercial value and trust.

I've watched capable senior planners talk themselves out of director jobs — all technical mastery, no commercial or people dimension — while a less dazzling rival who talked about winning work, growing staff and carrying risk took the offer. The panel wasn't choosing the better planner; it was choosing the one who knew which job they were interviewing for. Work out which conversation you're in, and have it.

title: Part 4 — The planning question bank
paras: Part four — the planning question bank. The written guide gives you a working bank of real interview questions, level by level, with what each is really testing — because the surface words and the thing being assessed are rarely the same. Prepare a genuine example for every question that applies to you.
Treat it as illustrative — representative of real UK planning interviews across the levels, in 2025 and 2026.

title: Part 5 — Technical questions
paras: Part five — technical questions. They test knowledge, but also whether you can apply it, and whether you'll bluff when you shouldn't. The gravest error is pretending to know something you don't — a confident wrong answer worries a panel far more than an honest 'I haven't dealt with that directly, but my understanding is this, and I'd check X'. Never bluff.
The depth expected rises with seniority, and at director level these are rarely the focus. Either way, confirm the current legal position before you rely on any technical detail.

title: Part 6 — Answering well: STAR, and standing out
paras: Part six — answering well. For any 'tell me about a time' question, reach for STAR. The Situation, briefly. The Task. The Action — the heart of it, always what you did, not what 'we' did. The Result, with a number where you honestly can. Use it for competency and scenario questions, not simple factual or opinion ones. And to not sound rehearsed: know your stories, not your scripts — six or seven real examples told naturally, not word-for-word answers that fall apart when the question's rephrased.

The difference, on one question — a member goes against your recommendation. The average answer: 'I'd be professional and accept the committee's decision.' True, but empty. The excellent answer gives a real case: an evidenced recommendation on a village housing scheme, refused by members on character grounds — then making the reasons defensible, backing the committee publicly, briefing the applicant honestly on appeal prospects, and defending it at appeal, where it was dismissed. Not taken personally: committees weigh things differently, and your job is advice that stands up either way.

That's the pattern. You show commercial awareness by talking value, fees, risk and delivery; judgement by how you weigh things; integrity by owning a mistake; calmness by how you discuss a crisis; leadership by the people you developed. Anyone can say 'I have excellent judgement' — only a good candidate proves it, with a case where their judgement was tested, and held.

title: Part 7 — Presentations and virtual interviews
paras: Part seven — presentations, and virtual interviews. Presentations first. Many senior and some mid-level interviews now include one — ten to fifteen minutes on a set brief, like how you'd grow the team, your approach to a live site, a market you'd target. It tests how you think, structure and communicate under pressure. Keep it simple: a clear opening that states your answer, three or four substantiated points, a short close back to the brief. Slides few and clean — six to ten, minimal text, one idea each. Rehearse to time; overrunning reads as poor judgement. Say the thing, prove it, stop.

Virtual interviews are routine now — Teams, Zoom, Meet — and a poor setup undercuts a strong candidate. A plain, tidy background. Camera at eye level. Light on your face from the front, not a window behind. A decent microphone, a tested connection. Eyes to the camera, not your own image. Dress as in person. Discreet notes off-camera are fine, but don't read from them. And if the technology fails, stay calm, suggest the phone, carry on — how you handle a glitch is itself a test of composure.

title: Part 8 — The questions you should ask
paras: Part eight — the questions you should ask. When they ask 'do you have any questions for us?', the wrong answer is no — it reads as disinterest, and wastes your best chance at a strong final impression. Some that work well.

What does success look like in the first year? — outcomes thinking, and it tells you how you'll be judged. The biggest challenges facing the team right now? — realism, and an honest answer. How is the team structured, and how does work come in? — commercial curiosity, strong in the private sector. Progression from here? — ambition beyond the job. How would you describe the culture, honestly? — fit matters to you too, and it often gets a candid reply. For a local authority, the service's priorities and pressures? — you understand the real context. And, anything about my experience to expand on? — confident, a last chance to close any doubt.
Two cautions. Don't let your only questions be pay, leave and hours — there's a time, and it isn't now. And never ask something a moment on their website would have answered.

title: Part 9 — What employers are really deciding
paras: Part nine — what employers are really deciding. Beneath every interview, whatever the questions, the panel is deciding a few very human things. Confidence against arrogance — quiet certainty impresses, bluster alarms. Professional judgement. Commercial thinking. Self-awareness and resilience. Integrity. Emotional intelligence. Technical ability gets you shortlisted; these get you hired. Really, the panel is silently asking trust questions.

Would we trust you with a difficult client, alone? Let you go to committee and speak for us? Be comfortable leaving you in front of an important developer, or a room of angry residents? Hand you the contentious case, and still sleep at night? Want to promote you — and would others follow you?
Everything you say builds or erodes the answer. A candidate who grasps this stops trying to impress and starts trying to reassure — which, paradoxically, is far more impressive.

title: Part 10 — Negotiating the offer
paras: Part ten — negotiating the offer. Negotiate after the offer, when your leverage is highest and they've decided they want you — not before. Know your whole package, and the market rate; the Salaries and Progression guide covers that. Be ready to discuss more than base pay — bonus, car allowance, pension, annual leave, hybrid working, professional subscriptions, training and C-P-D, promotion prospects, probation and notice. Ask professionally, from evidence, not from need; in a candidate's market a reasonable request rarely offends. And treat counter-offers from your current employer with caution — they solve the money but seldom the reasons you looked, and many who accept have moved on within the year. A good recruiter negotiates for you at arm's length.

title: Part 11 — Interview mistakes, ranked
paras: Part eleven — interview mistakes, ranked, from the ones that end a candidacy on the spot down to the habits that quietly cost offers. Most candidates make only one or two, without realising.

The serious ones, that end interviews: bluffing a technical answer; lying or exaggerating and getting caught; badmouthing an employer; breaching confidentiality on live cases or clients, which is instantly disqualifying; arrogance, dismissing others or talking over the panel; criticising a scheme the interviewer worked on; no research; being unable to talk through a single real case, fatal for an experienced planner; blaming others for every setback; and rudeness to junior staff or the recruiter.

The costly ones, that lose offers: rambling that never reaches a point; vague, 'we'-heavy answers; not knowing the authority's housing land supply or Local Plan position; at senior level, still proving technical competence instead of leadership; reciting policy instead of applying it; memorised answers that fall apart when rephrased; no questions, or only pay and leave; talking too much and never letting the panel steer, or too little; overrunning a presentation or reading the slides; a poor virtual setup; no concrete examples; negotiating hard before an offer exists; no genuine interest in this employer; and being unable to explain why you're leaving.

And the avoidable ones, that leave a dent: arriving flustered or logging on late; dressing too casually and misreading the formality; fidgeting, poor eye contact, low energy; not preparing questions, or asking something the website answers; not linking your answers to their role and needs; undue modesty, never saying what you achieved; waffling when you don't know; forgetting the interviewers' names or roles; no follow-up thank-you; and treating a so-called junior interviewer as unimportant.

title: Part 12 — The four-week preparation plan
paras: Part twelve — the four-week preparation plan. Preparation spread over a month beats a panic the night before, every time. Shorter notice? Just compress it proportionately.

title: The ten habits of highly employable planners
paras: And finally, the ten habits of highly employable planners. Interviews are won in the years before them, not the hour of them — the habits that separate the planners always in demand from the ones who struggle.

One, keep learning — C-P-D is a habit, not a box. Two, become known for something — a specialism, the one for energy consents, the one who wins hard appeals. Three, tell the truth, to clients, members, colleagues and interviewers; integrity is the foundation. Four, deliver, reliably, and finish what you start. Five, think commercially, even in the public sector — value, risk and delivery, not only policy. Six, stay calm, under pressure, in hostile rooms. Seven, help others — mentor, share, lift juniors — and be recommended warmly for it, for years. Eight, keep your reputation in order — C-V current, LinkedIn strong, footprint clean. Nine, build relationships before you need them. And ten, own your mistakes — admit, learn, move on — which is exactly what earns trust.

Do these steadily and the interview looks after itself. You'll walk in as someone the panel already half-wants to hire, and spend far less of your career chasing jobs — because the good ones come to find you.

One closing note. This guide was compiled in 2026, drawing on long UK planning-recruitment experience. The recruitment statistics quoted elsewhere in the Careers section are all attributed to their sources in the written guide. Interview practice evolves, so treat the craft here as informed guidance, and the technical detail as a prompt to confirm the current position before you rely on it.
